description:
A solo team by Izabel Passos, a software engineer who builds real-time data tools 

For this challenge, the team is building health-monitoring software for astronauts: tracking heart rate over time, connecting it to sleep and recovery, and giving clear guidance when something looks off,  first on the space station, then on the spacecraft.
summary: McCoy's Lab is a health application designed for use by astronauts who undertake long flights without onboard physicians. I developed this application to monitor resting pulse rate over time, relate it to sleep and recovery, and provide one instruction to do in case of any deviations: rest and measure again. Simulated sensor transmits resting measurement at regular intervals (every 15 seconds), and the astronaut can trigger Measure button whenever he or she wants. In case of deviation of pulse rate over 100 bpm, the application issues alarm and instructs to rest, remeasure, and get medical attention in case of persisting deviations. Home screen features seven vitals: heart rate, sleep, body temperature, blood pressure, blood oxygenation, blood glucose level, as well as the mood (reported via a smileys tap). Initially this application works on the space station, then it starts working on board spacecraft in LCARS interface of StarTrek movies. Below the chart is located McCoy's Note – a one-liner of doctor's analysis based on the live data from the application.
details:
I built McCoy's Lab for Challenge #4 because there is no doctor on board a long mission. The software has to do three things: track an indicator over time, show how it connects to sleep and recovery, and say clearly what to do first when something looks off. A LCARS interface with a nod to Dr. McCoy from The Original Series and a little tribute to Sir Patrick Stewart.

I started with resting heart rate. A simulated sensor sends a resting reading every 15 seconds (68–78 bpm in the demo), and the astronaut can press "Measure now" any time. The screen shows the latest reading, "Your normal", the average of the resting readings under 80 bpm and a chart of the last 10. If the latest reading goes over 100 bpm, the app shows "Elevated heart rate alert" and tells the astronaut to rest and measure again, and to seek medical care if it stays high. I chose the limits under 80 bpm for resting, over 100 for the alert as design choices for this prototype, and I say so in the app. Every reading is simulated crew data, labelled simulated. I did not use a real astronaut heart-rate series.

The interface is Star Trek: The Next Generation LCARS, built in pure CSS with Antonio font, colour-blocked frames, uppercase labels. The welcome screen has seven vitals: heart rate, sleep, body temperature, blood pressure, oxygenation, blood sugar, plus mood, which the astronaut logs by tapping one of five faces at the top of the chart box. Click a tile (or a mood face) and the centre chart switches to that vital. Heart rate is the live sensor series. Sleep, temperature, pressure, oxygenation and blood sugar are labelled simulated series: sleep is the last 7 nights; temperature runs 36.4–36.7 °C; systolic pressure 118–122; oxygenation 97–99%; blood sugar 90–110 mg/dL. Each has its own scale. Mood is a 1–5 series, logged by hand. Day 1 is the space station; Day 2 is the spacecraft, with its own aqua accent inside the orange LCARS frame. The tiles sit in a column on the left, the chart is a big centre screen, and the whole thing works down to phone width.

Below the chart there are two cards that a plain dashboard does not have. McCoy's Note is a one-line doctor's verdict, computed from the live readings: "All vitals steady — crew is fit for duty" when everything is in range, "Heart rate running a little high — keep an eye on it" between 80 and 100, and the rest-and-re-measure advice above 100. The Stardate card shows the current stardate (Stardate 41000 is the Enterprise-D's first year, 2364, and each year adds 1000) and the signal delay to Earth: about 12 minutes each way from the spacecraft, under 1 second from the station.

Under the hood it is React/TypeScript + Vite on the front, FastAPI on the back. The back end keeps readings in memory and serves GET /readings (latest reading, alert state, and the temperature, pressure, oxygenation, blood sugar and mood series), POST /measure (adds a reading 105 bpm in the demo fires the alert) and POST /mood (logs a mood check-in, 1–5). A back-end thread adds a simulated resting reading of 68–78 bpm every 15 seconds, keeping the last 60, and simulated temperature, pressure, oxygenation and blood sugar on the same cadence. The front polls /readings every 15 seconds. If the back end is down, the front falls back locally, so the demo keeps working.
projectRefs: Why Do We Conduct Science Experiments in Space?
